previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: The patient with prior Roux-en-Y gastric bypass presented with one day of epigastric pain with nausea and a single non-bloody, non-bilious emesis and increased loose stools. Evaluation included labs without leukocytosis, CT abdomen/pelvis showing oral contrast in both the gastric pouch and remnant suggesting possible fistulous communication and mild proximal efferent limb dilation without obstruction, and EGD demonstrating a widely patent gastrojejunostomy with two perianastomotic jejunal ulcers (one superficial clean-based and one deeper cratered ulcer) without active bleeding; H. pylori serology was negative. She was treated with IV morphine transitioned to oral oxycodone-acetaminophen solution, started on IV Protonix then transitioned to oral PPI, and her diet was advanced from Bariatric Stage 2 to Stage III with a lactose-free modification for diarrhea. With improved pain control and tolerance of oral intake/medications, she was discharged home on crushed omeprazole BID with return precautions and follow-up planning.
problems: Gastrojejunal ulcer, unspecified as acute or chronic, without mention of hemorrhage or perforation, without mention of obstruction

Brief Hospital Course:
Mrs. ___ presented to the Emergency Department the evening of 
___ with weakness following 7 days of inability to 
tolerate solids or liquids due to ongoing nausea.  Intravenous 
fluids, vitamins and electrolytes were administered and the 
patient was transferred to the general surgical ward for further 
management.

On hospital day #1 the patient continued to have epigastric pain 
and nausea which was managed with intravenous ondansetron.  
Intravenous pantoprazole was also resumed due to known 
ulcerations at the gastrojejunostomy, which was diagnosed on her 
previous admission.  

On hospital day #2 the epigastric pain improved significantly, 
but the nausea persisted.  Sucralfate therapy was initiated at 
this time.  On hospital day #3 the patient began having 
diarrhea.  Stool cultures were sent and intravenous fluids were 
resumed.  The following day stool cultures were negative for 
ova, parasites and campylobacter but positive clostridium 
difficile.  Oral metronidazole therapy was initiated.  

On hospital day #5 the patient was experiencing persistent 
diarrhea, therefore, Infectious Disease was consulted for 
recommendations regarding optimal managment of clostridium 
difficile in this patient.  They recommended continued oral 
metronidazole treatment for an initial 14-day period with 
potential for a longer treatment course given daily PPI 
requirments.  

As the hospital course progressed, the patient's diarrhea 
improved significantly.  Her nausea and epigastric pain 
completely resolved and she was able to ingest adequate amounts 
of protein, calories and fluids.

At the time of discharge, the patient was doing well, afebrile 
with stable vital signs.  The patient was tolerating a stage 3 
diet, ambulating, voiding without assistance, and without pain.  
The patient received discharge teaching and follow-up 
instructions with understanding verbalized and agreement with 
the discharge plan.

Discharge Diagnosis:
Clostridium difficile colitis

 
Discharge Condition:
Mental Status: Clear and coherent.
Level of Consciousness: Alert and interactive.
Activity Status: Ambulatory - Independent.

 
Discharge Instructions:
Discharge Instructions: Please call your surgeon or return to 
the emergency department if you develop a fever greater than 
101.5, chest pain, shortness of breath, severe abdominal pain, 
pain unrelieved by your pain medication, severe nausea or 
vomiting, severe abdominal bloating, inability to eat or drink, 
foul smelling or colorful drainage from your incisions, redness 
or swelling around your incisions, or any other symptoms which 
are concerning to you.

Diet: Stay on Stage III diet until your follow up appointment. 
Do not self advance
diet, do not drink out of a straw or chew gum.

Medication Instructions:
Resume your home medications, CRUSH ALL PILLS.
You will be starting some new medications:
1.  You are being discharged on medications to treat the pain 
from your operation. These medications will make you drowsy and 
impair your ability to drive a motor vehicle or operate 
machinery safely. You MUST refrain from such activities while 
taking these medications.
2. You should begin taking a chewable complete multivitamin with 
minerals. No gummy vitamins.
3. You must not use NSAIDS (non-steroidal anti-inflammatory 
drugs) Examples are Ibuprofen, Motrin, Aleve, Nuprin and 
Naproxen. These agents will cause bleeding and ulcers in your 
digestive system.

Activity:
No heavy lifting of items ___ pounds for 6 weeks. You may 
resume moderate exercise at your discretion, no abdominal 
exercises.

microbiology.test_name: CLOSTRIDIUM DIFFICILE TOXIN A & B TEST

microbiology.comments: NO OVA AND PARASITES SEEN.  This test does not reliably detect Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora or Microsporidium. While most cases of Giardia are detected by routine O+P, the Giardia antigen test may enhance detection when organisms are rare.
